title: Install a salvaged wood stove
summary: Set a found wood stove on a non-combustible pad at safe distances from walls, connect it with a short, rising stovepipe, and take the smoke out through an insulated chimney in the wall or roof. Missed clearances are a major cause of chimney fires and the connector pipe is the weak link; a window exit is not covered by any code and is weaker than a wall or roof exit.

materials.item: Floor pad: sheet steel at least 0.38 mm (0.015 in), or grouted tile or brick on a continuous non-combustible sheet
materials.qty: stove footprint plus 450 mm (18 in) in front and 200 mm (8 in) at the sides and back

materials.item: Black single-wall stovepipe, 24 gauge or heavier, the stove's outlet size (150 mm / 6 in on most)
Elbows: two 45° or at most two 90°, plus a telescopic length or inspection wrap
Insulated 650 °C chimney (ULC S629 or UL 103HT) with its wall thimble or ceiling support, tee and cleanout cap, wall bands, flashing, storm collar and cap
Heat shields: 24-gauge (0.61 mm) sheet steel on non-combustible spacers such as steel channel
Sheet steel to fill a window opening, for the window exit only
High-temperature silicone for the roof flashing
CO alarm and smoke alarm for the stove room

steps.text: Read the label on the back of the stove: it gives the clearances, pipe size and chimney type, and it overrides the manual (Drolet Part 1). No label: use the uncertified-stove distances in the notes (NRCan wood heating).

Pick the spot: the room you live in, with the chimney going straight up through the warm house rather than up an outside wall (NRCan wood heating). Every room people sleep in needs two ways out, and in a cold snap that includes the stove room: keep both clear, and don't count a window you plan to fill with steel (Ready.gov fires).
steps.warn: Not in the bedroom of a mobile home (Drolet Part 1). A basement stove can overfire or smoulder with nobody noticing (NRCan wood heating).

steps.text: Lay a continuous non-combustible floor pad reaching 450 mm (18 in) in front of the loading door and 200 mm (8 in) past the sides and back (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Escape 1800).
steps.warn: Never lay the pad on carpet unless it is supported so it can't bend or crack (NRCan wood heating). An unlabelled stove can also overheat the floor through its base, so for one the pad alone isn't enough (NRCan wood heating).

steps.text: Set the stove and measure to every wall and the ceiling. Where it's too close, fit a heat shield on non-combustible spacers with an air gap behind it (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Escape 1800).
steps.warn: The air gap does the work. Foil, tile or brick fixed flat to the wall gives no reduction in these rules.

steps.text: Plan the pipe: straight up is best. Keep it under 3 m (10 ft) long, with no more than two 90° elbows and rising at least 20 mm per metre (¼ in per ft) toward the chimney (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1).

Fit black 24-gauge pipe, crimped ends pointing down toward the stove, with three screws at every joint, including the stove collar and the chimney (NRCan wood heating). Include a telescopic length or inspection wrap so it can come apart (Drolet Part 1).
steps.warn: Never galvanised pipe: the coating vaporises into dangerous gas (NRCan wood heating). Keep it 450 mm (18 in) from anything that burns.

steps.text: Where the smoke leaves the room, change to insulated chimney with its own thimble or ceiling support (Drolet Part 1, DuraVent DTC).
steps.warn: Stovepipe is a connector only: it never goes through a ceiling, floor, attic, roof space, closet or hidden space (Drolet Part 1) or through any wall (Woodstock close clearance); only insulated chimney in its own thimble does.

steps.text: Wall exit: cut the opening the chimney maker gives (12 × 12 in for a 6 in DuraTech in a wood wall), fit the two halves of the wall thimble, and push the insulated length through so it sticks at least 125 mm (5 in) into the room (DuraVent DTC).
Outside, fit the tee with its cleanout cap on a wall support screwed into the studs, then stack chimney up the wall with a wall band every 2.4 m (8 ft) (DuraVent DTC).
steps.warn: Leave the chimney's clearance space empty: don't pack insulation round it (DuraVent DTC).

steps.text: Take it up past the roof: at least 1 m (3 ft) above where it leaves the roof and 60 cm (2 ft) higher than anything within 3 m (10 ft). Brace it if it stands more than 1.5 m (5 ft) above its last support. Fit the cap (NRCan wood heating, DuraVent DTC).
steps.warn: Roof work is fall work: ladder footed or tied off, never alone, in wind or in the dark (see the fall hazard card).

steps.text: Fit a smoke alarm on or near the ceiling at the exits from the stove room and a CO alarm in the room, and keep an ABC extinguisher close (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1). Glowing coals and ash keep making carbon monoxide after the flames die (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1), so keep the alarm working and the ash outdoors in a covered metal can.

First fire: if the house and chimney are cold, crack a window or door for a few minutes to start the draft, and don't run range hoods, bath fans or a dryer while lighting (Drolet Part 1). Burn small fires first and check every joint for smoke.
steps.warn: Red-glowing pipe means overfiring: close the air controls until it cools (DuraVent DTC).

steps.text: Inspect the pipe and chimney at least every two months in the heating season, and clean them when soot or creosote is 3 mm (⅛ in) thick (Drolet Part 1).

notes:
## Start with the label
A certified stove's label gives its clearances, pipe size and chimney type, and it overrides the manual and everything else (Drolet Part 1). Follow it exactly; it was tested. In Canada the installation code is CSA B365, and in the US NFPA 211, where no local code applies (Drolet Part 1). An unlabelled stove is uncertified and gets the bigger default distances below (NRCan wood heating). Check it over first: [Check and fix a found wood stove](#guides/repair_wood_stove).

## Clearances to anything that burns
| What | Clearance | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Certified stove | What the label says | Drolet Part 1 |
| Uncertified stove, unshielded | 1,200 mm (48 in) sides, back and loading side; 1,500 mm (60 in) above | NRCan wood heating (CSA B365) |
| Uncertified stove with its own jacket or shield, spaced 50 mm (2 in) off the body and open at top and bottom | 900 mm (36 in) sides and back; the loading side stays 1,200 mm (48 in) | NRCan wood heating |
| Older US figure for a radiant stove (1974-76 NFPA, in a 1986 note), shorter than Canada's: don't use it where B365 applies | 36 in (914 mm) to walls and ceiling | Purdue FNR-100 |
| Single-wall stovepipe | 450 mm (18 in); 225 mm (9 in) with a shield | NRCan wood heating |
| Double-wall stovepipe | Label, about 150 mm (6 in) | Woodstock close clearance |
| Insulated chimney | Label, 50 mm (2 in) for DuraTech | DuraVent DTC |

Measure from the stove's outer surface; a non-combustible covering over a wooden wall doesn't count as a non-combustible wall (NRCan wood heating). Firewood, paper, curtains and furniture burn too: keep them outside the same clearances as the walls (the label's, or 1,200 mm (48 in) for an unlabelled stove), because Drolet says not to store fuel within the stove's minimum clearances (Drolet Part 1). A flat 1 m (3 ft) is only the usual household rule for things near a stove (Georgian Bay). The uncertified figures come from the 2001 edition of CSA B365 as printed in NRCan's guide, and the same unshielded numbers appear in Ontario's 2010 code guide and a municipal guideline (Ontario 2010 guide, Highlands East). The current edition, CSA B365:25, replaced the 2017 one in 2025 and revised the clearance and shielding rules, but it isn't free to read (SCC B365 listing, Nimonik B365 preface). Treat these as the least room to give, and give more where you can.

## Heat shields
A shield works because air flows up the gap behind it and carries the heat away (NRCan wood heating). Build it like this (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Escape 1800):
- Sheet steel at least 24 gauge (0.61 mm) (Drolet's figure; the B365-01 table in NRCan says 29 gauge, so 24 is the heavier choice), or tile or brick, on **non-combustible spacers**: 25 mm (1 in) of air behind it, or 21 mm (⅞ in) in Canada.
- A gap of 25 to 75 mm (1 to 3 in) at the bottom and at least 75 mm (3 in) at the top, so air can flow through.
- Extend it 450 mm (18 in) past each side of the stove and 500 mm (20 in) above it.
- Screws that go through the shield into the wall may be used only at the shield's edges, and none within 200 mm (8 in) of the stove's centre line.
- Steel wall strapping (light channel) makes good spacers; notch the bottom so air gets in (NRCan wood heating).

| Shield on spacers | Cut side and back clearance by | Cut ceiling clearance by |
|---|---|---|
| Sheet steel | 67% | 50% |
| Tile on non-combustible board | 50% | 33% |
| Tile on board backed with sheet steel | 67% | 50% |
| Brick | 50% | not listed |
| Brick backed with sheet steel | 67% | not listed |

Source: NRCan wood heating, Drolet Escape 1800. So an uncertified stove's 1,200 mm (48 in) with a steel shield comes down to about 400 mm (16 in). Brick or stone alone isn't suitable protection (Purdue FNR-100), and nothing fixed flat without the gap earns a reduction in these tables. A free-standing panel doesn't count; shields must be fixed to the wall (NRCan wood heating).

## Floor pad
A certified stove keeps the floor cool enough, but embers fall out when you load it. The pad must be one continuous non-combustible surface: sheet metal, grouted tile or mortared brick (NRCan wood heating). Drolet calls for steel at least 0.38 mm (0.015 in), and any tile needs a continuous non-combustible sheet under it in case it cracks; no pad is needed on bare concrete (Drolet Escape 1800). Size: 450 mm (18 in) in front of the loading door and 200 mm (8 in) round the rest (NRCan wood heating).

An uncertified stove can scorch the floor through its bottom, and NRCan says its floor protection depends on the leg height and any bottom protection (NRCan wood heating). Ontario's 2010 code guide pictures three set-ups for a non-listed stove: on hollow masonry units, on two metal plates with an air space between, or on a single 0.38 mm (15 mil) metal sheet with the stove standing at least about 175 mm (7 in) off it (read from a drawing in the Ontario 2010 guide; check the stove's label). The older US extension rule is looser (legs under 15 cm (6 in) need 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) of hollow masonry over 24-gauge sheet metal; legs of 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in) are better) (Purdue FNR-100), so use the Canadian one.

## The stovepipe
The connector pipe has been called the weak link of wood heating, because badly fitted pipe causes house fires (Drolet Part 1). The rules (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1):
- Same diameter as the stove's flue collar; black-painted, at least 24 gauge for 150, 175 and 200 mm (6, 7, 8 in) pipe. No galvanised pipe.
- Crimped (male) ends toward the stove, so dripping creosote and condensate stay inside.
- Three screws in every joint, including at the stove and the chimney.
- At most 3 m (10 ft) of pipe; no more than 1 m (3 ft) unsupported sideways; no more than two 90° elbows. Two 45° elbows beat one 90° (Drolet Part 1).
- Rising at least 20 mm per metre (¼ in per ft) toward the chimney.
- A telescopic length or inspection wrap, so it can expand and be taken down for cleaning without moving the stove.

Double-wall stovepipe needs less clearance and keeps the smoke hotter, but it is still a connector: it never passes through a wall or ceiling (Woodstock close clearance).

## Through a wall or ceiling
Stovepipe must never pass through a combustible floor or ceiling, an attic, a roof space, a closet or any hidden space (Drolet Part 1). Through a combustible wall the code (CSA B365) sets the method (Drolet Part 1): the usual one is insulated chimney in its own wall thimble (DuraVent DTC), and a pipe into a masonry chimney through a combustible wall needs an insulated listed thimble (Drolet Part 1). Insulated 650 °C chimney, often called Class A (Cornell wood stove safety), is marked ULC S629 in Canada or UL 103HT in the US (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1); use only the parts made for that brand (Drolet Part 1). An old Type A metal chimney (used before 1983, built for oil furnaces) is not suitable for wood (NRCan wood heating). Gas B-vent is for listed gas appliances only (DuraVent B-vent), galvanised pipe and duct are out (NRCan wood heating), and Drolet warns against makeshift materials, so dryer duct and the like aren't stovepipe either (Drolet Part 1). For a 150 mm (6 in) DuraTech chimney in a wood-framed wall, the opening is 12 × 12 in, the thimble adjusts for walls 7 to 12 in thick, and the tee outside carries a cleanout cap (DuraVent DTC). Going up inside through a ceiling takes the maker's ceiling support or firestop, an attic radiation shield, and a 2 in (50 mm) gap at the roof (DuraVent DTC). See [Spot likely asbestos](#guides/safety_asbestos_check) before cutting into an old wall.

## Chimney height: the 3-2-10 rule
The top must be at least 1 m (3 ft) above where the chimney leaves the roof, and at least 60 cm (2 ft) higher than any roof, wall or building within 3 m (10 ft) (NRCan wood heating, DuraVent DTC). This is called the 3-2-10 rule (Flue-Pipes window). It gets the top above the wind eddies round the roof; trees and nearby houses may mean going higher (NRCan wood heating). As a rule of thumb, the whole system from the stove's floor to the chimney top should be at least 4.6 m (15 ft) (NRCan wood heating); Drolet asks for 3.66 m (12 ft) from the stove top (Drolet Part 1).

A chimney up an outside wall is cold. It draws weakly, collects more creosote and can pull cold air and smoke down into the house when no fire is burning (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1). Go up through the warm house where you can.

## An existing masonry chimney
It needs a clay or listed stainless liner (Drolet Part 1). The pipe goes into a thimble that must not stick out past the inner surface of the liner (Missouri chimneys). One stove per flue, and not into a fireplace flue (Drolet Part 1, Missouri chimneys). Check it first: [Check a chimney](#guides/test_chimney).

## Through a window: don't, if there is another way
The US model code (IRC) doesn't allow stovepipe out through a window, its glass or its frame, and a metal plate in place of the glass passes only if the plate is itself listed for passing through a wall. The same source sends the chimney through the solid wall beside the window or straight up through the roof instead, and says window plate kits sold for tent stoves exist and must be judged by their label (Flue-Pipes window). Do that, with the maker's thimble and insulated chimney as in the wall exit above.

No code or maker's manual covers an improvised window exit, so what follows is not a tested assembly. It is the least-bad version if the only alternative is freezing, and it is weaker than a wall or roof exit:
- **Take out the sash and glass** and fill the whole opening with sheet steel fixed to the frame.
- **Single-wall pipe:** every bit of wood, frame and siding must stay 450 mm (18 in) from the pipe (NRCan wood heating). For a 150 mm (6 in) pipe that means a clear steel panel about 1,070 mm (42 in) across: the pipe plus 450 mm each side. Most windows are smaller, and then it can't be made safe.
- **Insulated chimney through the steel** keeps its labelled clearance from the wooden frame (50 mm, 2 in, for DuraTech), but DuraVent's wall thimble is made for a framed wall opening (12 × 12 in for 6 in DuraTech), not a steel plate in a window (DuraVent DTC).
- **Outside**, carry on as for a wall exit: tee with a cleanout cap, a wall support, bands, and up to the 3-2-10 height (DuraVent DTC, NRCan wood heating).

What it can't make safe: a pipe that pokes out and stops below the roof edge sits in the wind eddies round the house, draws badly and lets smoke into the room when you light it (NRCan wood heating). The outside run is cold and makes creosote (NRCan wood heating).

You also lose the window as a way out. Every room people sleep in needs two ways out (Ready.gov fires), and in a cold snap that includes the stove room: a window filled with steel and a hot pipe outside is not one of them. Don't use the escape window of any bedroom, and keep the stove room's other way out clear. These sources don't cover tents, campers or earth walls; the connector-only rule above still holds (Woodstock close clearance).

## Air, alarms and the first fire
Room air is the best combustion air, but range hoods, bath fans, dryers and central vacuums can pull the house negative and spill smoke; avoid running them while lighting (Drolet Part 1). Never hook a stove to furnace ducts or under a hood: the chimney flow can reverse and fill the house with smoke (NRCan wood heating). A CO alarm and a smoke alarm are required in the stove's room (Drolet Part 1); put smoke alarms on or near the ceiling at the room's exits (NRCan wood heating), and outside each sleeping area and on every level (Georgian Bay). A smoke alarm near the stove may go off when you open the door (Drolet Part 1). Glowing coals and ash keep making CO after the flames die (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1). See [carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide) for what CO alarms can and can't tell you.

## Upkeep
Check the pipe and chimney at least every two months in the season, and monthly until you know how fast creosote builds; 3 mm (⅛ in) of soot or creosote means clean it now (Drolet Part 1). See [chimney sweeping](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping) and [what to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn).
